lessonRef.subject: mathematics
lessonRef.focus: building and reading two-way frequency tables
lessonRef.title: Performance task planning: building and reading two-way frequency tables

sections.title: Instructional examples
sections.directions: This example shows how to justify a modelling choice.

items.prompt: Group X: 12 successes, 8 failures. Find P(success | X).

sections.title: Guided practice
sections.directions: Decide what the quantities are before you compute anything.

items.prompt: Two events have P(A) = 8/10, P(B) = 9/10, and P(A and B) = 77/100. Are A and B independent?
choices: No; P(A and B) differs from P(A)·P(B).
Yes; P(A and B) equals P(A)·P(B).
No; the two events are mutually exclusive.
Yes; the two events cannot occur together.

items.prompt: In a group of 38, 20 do activity A, 20 do activity B, and 10 do both. Find P(A or B) as a fraction in lowest terms.
An event has probability 6/7 on a single trial. Two independent trials are run. Find the probability of at least one success, as a fraction in lowest terms.

sections.title: Extension and challenge
sections.directions: Plan in writing: what you will model, why that model, and how you will check it.

items.prompt: A survey table records: group X with 28 successes and 21 failures; group Y with 40 successes and 29 failures. Find P(success | group X) as a fraction in lowest terms.
items.responseExpectation: Give the result and the reasoning that produced it. Show enough work that someone else could check each step.

items.prompt: Two events have P(A) = 8/10, P(B) = 6/10, and P(A and B) = 48/100. Are A and B independent?
items.responseExpectation: Give the result and the reasoning that produced it. Show enough work that someone else could check each step.

items.prompt: In a group of 62, 32 do activity A, 40 do activity B, and 17 do both. Find P(A or B) as a fraction in lowest terms.
items.responseExpectation: Give the result and the reasoning that produced it. Show enough work that someone else could check each step.
